title: fix: iterate grid-installed groups in applyContentRightInset (fixes #337477)
text: fix: iterate grid-installed groups in applyContentRightInset (fixes #337477). ### Summary `EditorPart.applyContentRightInset()` iterates every group in the `groupViews` map and asks the grid for each group's right-hand neighbors. During grid reconstruction (state restore / layout apply), `doCreateGroupView()` inserts freshly-created group views into `groupViews` *before* the rebuilt `SerializableGrid` is installed via `doSetGridWidget()`. A re-entrant active-editor-change event fired from inside the deserialize callback flows through the Agents-window single-pane layer back into `applyContentRightInset()`, which then queries the still-old `gridWidget` for a group it does not contain, so `Grid.getViewLocation()` throws `Error: View not found`. Impact: an unhandled error is reported on Windows and Mac during Agents-window working-set / grid restore. Fixes microsoft/vscode\#337477 Recommended reviewer: `@sandy081` ### Culprit Commit | Field | Value | |-------|-------| | Commit | `7317e60f

title: Sessions: Polish layout when many related session pills are shown
text: Sessions: Polish layout when many related session pills are shown. When a session interacts with many other sessions, the related-session pills are displayed in a tall vertical stack. This consumes a lot of space and makes the session UI feel visually cluttered. It would be good to use a more compact presentation for larger sets of related sessions, for example wrapping the pills horizontally or collapsing overflow behind a summary affordance. ## Steps to reproduce 1. Open a session that has interacted with several other sessions. 2. View the related-session pills. 3. Notice that the pills are stacked vertically and dominate the layout. ## Expected Related sessions remain easy to scan and open without producing a tall vertical stack.

title: Agents window stalls after Copilot runtime panic during MCP/plugin refresh
text: Agents window stalls after Copilot runtime panic during MCP/plugin refresh. Existing chats in the Agents window stalled on every request and reported unavailable models, even though GitHub authentication and model discovery succeeded. During MCP/plugin refresh (`reason=clientPluginsChanged`), the shared Copilot runtime crashed: Subsequent requests stalled or failed with `Connection is closed`, affecting other chats too. **Workaround:** I disabled `component-explorer`, `vscode-automation-mcp`, and Azure MCP in the affected chats, then restarted Insiders. The existing chats responded again without clearing history or disabling sandbox protections. Rolling back to the previous Insiders build had not helped. **Expected:** A failing MCP integration should not crash the shared runtime and prevent other chats from using models. **Environment:** macOS Apple Silicon; Insiders `1.140.0-insider` (`9cc2a44`); Copilot Chat `0.68.2026092302`.

title: fix: only show banner message hover when truncated (build fix for vscode-engineering#3943)
text: fix: only show banner message hover when truncated (build fix for vscode-engineering#3943). ## Build failure The `Run Sanity Tests` task timed out on every platform during the `installExtension` step. Playwright reported the Extensions view **Refresh** button as visible, enabled, and stable, but every click was blocked because the Restricted Mode banner's tooltip overlay intercepted the pointer events: ## Root cause `src/vs/workbench/browser/parts/banner/bannerPart.ts` was recently updated to attach a delayed hover to the banner message container: Because the banner code is shared, this also applies to the existing Restricted Mode banner. The hover fired unconditionally on mouse-over, popping a hover overlay even when the message was not truncated. That overlay is positioned over the workbench and intercepts pointer events on controls directly below the banner — including the Extensions **Refresh** button — so clicks never land. The `.message-container` already truncates overflowing te

title: fix: only show banner message hover when truncated (build fix for vscode-engineering#3943)
text: ectly below the banner — including the Extensions **Refresh** button — so clicks never land. The `.message-container` already truncates overflowing text (`text-overflow: ellipsis; white-space: nowrap; overflow: hidden`), so revealing the message on hover is only meaningful when the message is actually clipped. ## How the fix works The hover options are now provided lazily and only supply content when the message container is actually truncated (`scrollWidth > clientWidth`): When the message fits, the content resolves to an empty string, and `HoverService` short-circuits empty-content hovers (`_createHover` returns early for `content === ''`), so no overlay is created and pointer events pass through to controls below. When the message is truncated, the full text is still revealed on hover as intended. This preserves the accessibility/reveal behavior while removing the unconditional overlay. ## Rollback evaluation - Recommendation: **Do not roll back.** - Public culprit commit/PR: commit

text: Support rich text and Markdown tables for AI agent conversations in the integrated terminal. Feature request Add an optional rich-text rendering mode within the integrated terminal that: Renders Markdown tables with aligned columns and readable cell wrapping. Formats headings, bold text, lists, and code blocks. Updates as the agent streams its response. Allows switching between formatted and raw output. The conversation should remain interactive in the same terminal, without copying text, saving Markdown files, or opening a separate preview. title: Markdown editor: let extensions add syntax, like markdown.markdownItPlugins does for the preview
text: Markdown editor: let extensions add syntax, like markdown.markdownItPlugins does for the preview. Extensions cannot add Markdown syntax to the new Markdown editor (`vscode.markdown.editor`). The preview has `markdown.markdownItPlugins`, and many extensions use it to add syntax: footnotes, admonitions, wiki links, definition lists, emoji shortcodes, and so on. The editor parses with micromark through `@vscode/markdown-editor` and has its own view, so none of those plugins reach it. Checked in 1.137.0. The editor bundle (`markdown-editor-out/editor.js`) has no reference to `markdownItPlugins`. As far as I can find, the only extension point the editor has is `markdown.codeBlockEditorProviders`. It replaces the view of fenced code blocks that match a selector. That helps for diagram-style blocks. It does nothing for inline syntax or for block syntax outside a code fence. The result is that a document that renders correctly in the preview, with the user's installed extensions, renders diffe

title: Markdown editor: let extensions add syntax, like markdown.markdownItPlugins does for the preview
text: syntax outside a code fence. The result is that a document that renders correctly in the preview, with the user's installed extensions, renders differently in the editor, and extension authors have no way to close that gap. #337447 (footnotes) is one case of this. Each missing construct now needs its own request against the built-in package. Requested: a contribution point that lets an extension add syntax to the editor. Two possible ways: - Accept micromark syntax extensions plus a matching rendering and serialisation hook. This is the closest match to how the editor parses today, and micromark's extension format is already public. - A narrower version: let an extension claim a node type or an inline pattern and render it read-only, while the source text round-trips unchanged. That would cover most preview plugins, whose output is display-only. Whichever is chosen, the source text must round-trip unchanged when a user edits around the extended syntax, so that installing an extension

GitHub renders the same file with a superscript link and a footnotes section at the end. Checked in VS Code 1.137.0 (Linux). The versions of `@vscode/markdown-editor` bundled in 1.137 (0.0.2-88), 1.138 (0.0.2-95) and 1.139 (0.0.2-107), and the latest on npm (0.0.2-108), all have no footnote support. The package loads micromark with frontmatter, gfm-table, gfm-task-list-item, gfm-strikethrough and math. title: Agent Host: Claude sessions are never reaped — 91 orphaned `claude` processes after 8 days, plus O(n) state broadcasts to unknown sessions
text: Agent Host: Claude sessions are never reaped — 91 orphaned `claude` processes after 8 days, plus O(n) state broadcasts to unknown sessions. # Agent Host: Claude sessions are never reaped — 91 orphaned `claude` processes after 8 days, plus O(n) state broadcasts to unknown sessions ## Environment - VS Code: 1.137.0 - OS: macOS 26.6.2, Apple M4 Max (Mac16,5), 36 GB RAM - Agent host plugin: `vscode-synced-customization-agent-host-claude-*` - Claude Agent SDK: `0.3.258` (also present in cache: `0.3.220`, `0.3.239`) - Single VS Code window, uptime 8 days, ~7 workspaces used ## Summary The agent host never terminates the `claude` child process backing a chat session when that session is closed. Over 8 days of normal use (~11 conversations/day) this accumulated **91 live `claude` processes**, all children of the same extension host process, holding ~8 GB RSS. Separately, `AgentHostStateManager` broadcasts session actions to sessions it no longer recognises, logging `Action for unknown session`

title: Agent Host: Claude sessions are never reaped — 91 orphaned `claude` processes after 8 days, plus O(n) state broadcasts to unknown sessions
text: ng ~8 GB RSS. Separately, `AgentHostStateManager` broadcasts session actions to sessions it no longer recognises, logging `Action for unknown session` once per session per event. With 156 leaked session references this turns a single customization change into tens of thousands of log lines and wakes every orphaned process at once. The two compound: the leak grows `n`, and every broadcast costs O(n). ## Observed behaviour ### 1. Child processes outlive their sessions 91 `claude` processes, all with the same PPID (the agent host utility process), ages ranging from minutes to the full 8-day lifetime of the window: Breakdown by age: 74 older than 24 h, 14 between 1 h and 24 h, 3 under 1 h. The oldest matches the window's own start time — nothing had ever been reaped. Extracting `--resume= ` from all of them gives **56 UUIDs, 56 distinct sessions, zero duplicates**. So this is not one session respawning after a crash: it is one never-terminated process per conversation ever opened. Closing

title: Agent Host: Claude sessions are never reaped — 91 orphaned `claude` processes after 8 days, plus O(n) state broadcasts to unknown sessions
text: ons, zero duplicates**. So this is not one session respawning after a crash: it is one never-terminated process per conversation ever opened. Closing the window does clean up correctly — all 91 exited with their parent, no processes reparented to launchd. The leak is purely per-session, not on shutdown. ### 2. `Action for unknown session` broadcast storm Over the window's lifetime: **73,875 occurrences**, of which **73,863** are `session/customizationsChanged`, spread across **156 distinct session ids**. These are not evenly distributed — they arrive in bursts: | Date | Occurrences | |---|---| | 2026-09-17 | 133 | | 2026-09-18 | 79 | | 2026-09-19 | 64 | | 2026-09-20 | 80 | | 2026-09-21 | 10 | | 2026-09-22 | 408 | | **2026-09-23** | **73,101** | The final burst is concentrated in ~10 seconds, peaking at **19,138 lines in a single second** (10:35:46). Accompanied by: (54 occurrences, across 216 distinct `Claude: ` references.) It looks like one customization change fans out to every trac

title: Agent Host: Claude sessions are never reaped — 91 orphaned `claude` processes after 8 days, plus O(n) state broadcasts to unknown sessions
text: (10:35:46). Accompanied by: (54 occurrences, across 216 distinct `Claude: ` references.) It looks like one customization change fans out to every tracked session, including the ones the state manager itself reports as unknown, with no guard and no upper bound. ## Impact Steady state, the leak is quiet — 37.7 h of cumulative CPU across 17,472 process-hours of lifetime is ~0.2 % average, so the orphans are mostly idle. **The cost is memory**: ~8 GB of RSS permanently held, which on a 36 GB machine is enough to push the system into compressor/swap. When a broadcast storm hits, every orphan is woken at once on an already memory-starved machine: | Metric | During | After closing VS Code | |---|---|---| | CPU idle | 6 % | 94 % | | CPU in system mode | 75 % | 2.7 % | | `kernel_task` | 277 % | negligible | | Free RAM | 48 MB | 17 GB | | Compressor | 17 GB | 5.6 GB | | Swap used | 12.6 / 13.3 GB | 3.6 GB | | Load average | 65 | ~2 | | Processes in uninterruptible I/O | 43 | 0 | The machine beca

title: Agent Host: Claude sessions are never reaped — 91 orphaned `claude` processes after 8 days, plus O(n) state broadcasts to unknown sessions
text: r | 17 GB | 5.6 GB | | Swap used | 12.6 / 13.3 GB | 3.6 GB | | Load average | 65 | ~2 | | Processes in uninterruptible I/O | 43 | 0 | The machine became unusable — not from CPU saturation but from memory thrashing, the kernel spending 75 % of CPU compressing and decompressing pages. Closing the VS Code window resolved it instantly and completely. ## Steps to reproduce 1. Open VS Code and leave the window running for several days. 2. Open Claude agent sessions across several workspaces, a handful per day, closing each chat when done. 3. Periodically run `pgrep -fc 'agent-host/sdk-cache'` — the count only ever increases, including for chats closed days earlier. 4. Watch `Action for unknown session` accumulate in `~/Library/Application Support/Code/logs/ /agenthost*.log`. 5. Observe system memory pressure (`vm_stat`, `sysctl vm.swapusage`) degrade over days. ## Expected - Closing a chat session terminates its `claude` child process, or the agent host reaps processes whose session is gone.

title: Agent Host: Claude sessions are never reaped — 91 orphaned `claude` processes after 8 days, plus O(n) state broadcasts to unknown sessions
text: egrade over days. ## Expected - Closing a chat session terminates its `claude` child process, or the agent host reaps processes whose session is gone. - `AgentHostStateManager` drops references to unknown sessions rather than broadcasting to them indefinitely — an unknown session should be unregistered on first miss, not re-warned tens of thousands of times. ## Notes - `~/Library/Application Support/Code/agentPlugins/` holds 16 stacked versions of the agent host plugin and 3 SDK versions, so behaviour may vary by version. - Possibly related: #337153, #334159, #332073 (agent host session lifecycle), #307401 (listener leak, renderer CPU), #334421 (extension host CPU/RAM growth). None of them describe process accumulation or the unknown-session broadcast.

title: Automation sessions briefly flicker in the Sessions list
text: Automation sessions briefly flicker in the Sessions list. ### Type of issue Bug ### Description Automation sessions briefly appear in the Sessions list for 1–2 seconds and then disappear again. This makes the Sessions list visibly flicker. This happens both when opening the Agents window and when restarting the local Agent Host. ### Steps to reproduce 1. Open one or more repositories that have non-archived automation sessions. 2. Open the Agents window and watch the Sessions list. 3. Run the **Developer: Restart Local Agent Host** command. 4. Watch the Sessions list while the Agent Host restarts. ### Actual behavior Automation sessions briefly show in the Sessions list for 1–2 seconds, causing the list to flicker, and then disappear again. ### Expected behavior Automation sessions that should be filtered out should never appear in the Sessions list, including while the Agents window is initializing or the local Agent Host is restarting.

Linux (repro'd while connected to a Dev Container / remote session; unclear if remote-specific) - Feature (e.g. agent/edit/ask mode): Chat windows - Selected model (e.g. GPT 4.1, Claude 3.7 Sonnet): Auto - Logs: none found Steps to Reproduce: 1. Open the Chat view in the sidebar (not as an editor tab). 2. In the Sessions list, select an existing chat. 3. Right click-it and choose Rename to rename it. 4. Type a new name and press Enter. Expected behavior: The chat session's name updates to the new value. Actual behavior: The name is not changed — the rename is silently dropped. No error or notification is shown. This happens all the time and persists across restarts of VS Code (not a one-off transient state issue). Workaround found: The same steps lead to a chat rename

title: Renaming a chat session in the Chat sidebar fails silently
text: ens all the time and persists across restarts of VS Code (not a one-off transient state issue). Workaround found: The same steps lead to a chat rename reliably when the same chat is opened as an editor tab (e.g., via "Open Chat in Editor"). It does not have to be the focused tab. It only fails when the chat is not opened as an editor tab. Additional notes: No relevant log output found in the GitHub Copilot Chat extension log or exthost logs when the failure occurs — suggests the failure is in the base VS Code Chat sessions tree/list UI, not the Copilot Chat extension itself. Suspect the inline rename input in the sidebar tree view is being torn down by a concurrent list re-render (e.g., a periodic "Sessions" refresh) before the new name is committed/persisted, causing the edit to be lost without error.

title: Agents window hangs with thousands of binary text models and a stale origin/HEAD base branch
text: Agents window hangs with thousands of binary text models and a stale origin/HEAD base branch. Its reported branch comparison was `vnext → master`, even though the repository's actual default branch is `main`. The local `origin/HEAD` still pointed to obsolete `origin/master`, at a 2021 commit. That comparison covers **9,883 files**. During the hang, logs show thousands of diagnostic updates for agent-host resources and sustained creation/disposal of text models for PNG/GIF/MP4 files. The Agents renderer reached roughly **200% CPU and 8-9

The Agents renderer reached roughly **200% CPU and 8-9 GB memory**, and its extension host roughly **100-110% CPU**. The stale base branch is a strong candidate trigger for the excessive work. Five-second native samples of both hot processes showed activity in V8/JavaScript execution. They did not provide symbolized JavaScript stacks sufficient to identify the responsible function. ### Incident-specific log counts Across the rotated window-1 extension-host logs, filtering to **2026-09-23 08:xx**, `vscode.extension-editing` diagnostic updates for `vscode-agent-host://` resources yielded: - **2,759 diagnostic batches**, from 08:28:41.977 through 08:33:47.117. - **1,491 distinct resource paths**, all associated with the same session. - These included **1,431 PNGs, 21 GIFs, 29 MP4s, and 8 JPGs**. These counts alone do not distinguish a finite backlog from a repeating loop. ## Expected behavior / investigation areas - Handle large branch comparisons without freezing the Agents window or eagerly materializing thousands of binary resources as text models. - Investigate how the session base branch is selected when local `origin/HEAD` is stale and the hosted repository's default branch has changed. - Determine what initiates this resource loading for an idle session and whether it can be bounded, lazy, or cancelled. ## Potential workaround (not yet verified) Repair the local remote-HEAD

title: Agent Host: verify OTLP trace endpoint routing and governed identity
text: Agent Host: verify OTLP trace endpoint routing and governed identity. Follow-up to #336814 (Local Copilot Chat identity capture). In a local Copilot Agent Host test, a base endpoint (`http://localhost:4318`) was copied into `OTEL_EXPORTER_OTLP_TRACES_ENDPOINT`. The runtime consequently posted traces to `/`, while the test collector accepted `/v1/traces`. Local Chat constructs the signal path explicitly. - Reproduce with an official OpenTelemetry Collector and the bundled Copilot runtime. - Correct base-versus-signal endpoint handling without breaking explicit/custom URLs, policy precedence, authentication, or existing metrics/logs and DB-mode routing. - Validate native governed identity independently of content capture, including denial and re-enable/restart behavior. Keep this separate from #336814; do not broadly rewrite customer endpoint URLs.

title: Cross-provider model delegation for BYOK/custom providers in Chat
text: Cross-provider model delegation for BYOK/custom providers in Chat. ## Describe the feature Allow models from different configured providers to call each other within a single Chat/Agent session. Today those providers can only be selected manually in the model picker — the agent cannot invoke them. ## Proposal Expose all configured models (Copilot-native and BYOK) as agent-invokable tools, e.g. `call_model(providerId, p

text: Prompt-to-skill migration fails with vague git pathspec error. ## Type of Issue Bug ## Description Converting several workspace prompts into skills fails with a low-level git error instead of completing the migration or explaining how to recover. text: 2 | Link showing `user@example.com` | Address is missing | | 3 | `snake_case, 2 * 3, [not a link]` | Escaped characters are missing: `snake case, 2 3, not a link` | | 4 | `AT&T, © 2026, #42` | Referenced characters are missing: `AT T, 2026, 42` | | 5 | H₂O with a subscript; `Ctrl` as a key | Tags are dropped and only their inner text remains: `H 2 O, press Ctrl` | | 6 | Link | Link (correct) | No related errors or warnings appear in the Developer Tools console (including the Markdown Editor webview's output). ### Likely cause This report was drafted with help from Claude Code (an AI assistant), including the source analysis below. I reproduced and verified all of the behavior in the table myself. I have not built the editor from source; this is from reading the shipped bundle, `extensions/markdown-language-features/markdown-editor-out/editor.js`. Parsing looks fine. The micromark text constructs register both `autolink` and `htmlText` for `<`, so the tokens are produced. However, the e

title: Markdown Editor: autolinks, backslash escapes, character references, and inline HTML disappear from rendered text
text: tor.js`. Parsing looks fine. The micromark text constructs register both `autolink` and `htmlText` for `<`, so the tokens are produced. However, the editor's inline AST builder (`_parseInlineEvent`) only dispatches `enter` events for `strongSequence`/`emphasisSequence`, `codeText`, `mathText`, `link`, `image`, `strikethrough`, `hardBreakTrailing`/`hardBreakEscape`, and `blockQuotePrefix`. Otherwise, it only creates text nodes on the `exit` of `data` or `codeTextData` tokens. As a result, the content of these tokens is silently skipped: - autolinks: `autolinkProtocol`, `autolinkEmail` - backslash escapes: `characterEscapeValue` - character references: `characterReferenceValue` - inline HTML: `htmlText` / `htmlTextData` The issues with the above are reported together because they appear to share the single cause given in this section; I'm happy to split them into separate issues if that's preferred. ### Related #334935 reports that `\$`, `$`, and `$` disappear in the Markdown

text: Zsh terminal revive reuses VS Code temporary ZDOTDIR as USER_ZDOTDIR. ## Type: Bug When a persistent zsh terminal is revived after restarting VS Code, VS Code's temporary shell-integration `ZDOTDIR` is reused as the user's `USER_ZDOTDIR`. This prevents the revived shell from loading the user's normal zsh configuration. ## Steps to reproduce 1. Use zsh in the integrated terminal with shell integration enabled. 2. Keep the terminal open and exit VS Code. 3. Start VS Code again and let the persistent terminal be revived. 4. After `History restored`, check: ## Actual result Both variables point to VS Code's temporary shell-integration directory: The user's normal `.zshrc` is not loaded correctly. title: Zsh terminal revive reuses VS Code temporary ZDOTDIR as USER_ZDOTDIR

Interpreter selection: a bare `bash` reaches WSL, not Git Bash `shell: "bash"` / a command starting with `bash` resolves through `PATH` to `C:\Windows\System32\bash.exe`, the WSL launcher. text: documents that `CreateProcess` gives the system directory precedence over `PATH`, so `System32\bash.exe` wins regardless of where Git Bash sits. The choice therefore has to be made by the hook executor. For comparison, Claude Code's hooks documentation states that shell-form hooks use "Git Bash on Windows" (https://code.claude.com/docs/en/hooks), and the measured behavior matches that statement. VS Code's hooks documentation does not state which shell runs a hook command, on Windows or on any other platform, so there is no documented contract to check an implementation against. microsoft/vscode#312314 points at `extensions/copilot/src/platform/chat/node/hookExecutor.ts` hardcoding the Windows shell, which looks like the same code path. ## 2. Verified independently under WSL bash on the same machine: a *quoted* Windows path keeps its backslashes and simply fails to resolve (a different error), while an *unquoted* one is mangled in exactly the way the hook log shows. The mangling is therefore evidence that the quotes are stripped upstream of bash, not that bash mishandled a quoted argument. Claude Code substitutes the same variable with forward slashes, so even if its quoting behaved identically there would be nothing for bash to consume. Measured: a script launched by a plugin-declared hook reports `CLAUDE_PLUGIN_ROOT` as unset. Under Claude Code the same script sees it set. This means the documented fallback — reading the env var instead of relying on token substitution — is not available, so defect 2 has no workaround from inside the script. *Hypothesis, not a finding:* because the interpreter is WSL (defect 1), Windows environment variables do not cross the interop boundary unless named in `WSLENV`, which would explain the variable disappearing even if the harness does set it on the spawned process. I have not confirmed this; it is offered only as a lead, and the observation stands regardless of the cause. ## Additional finding: `${...}` substitution is name-exact and destroys shell parameter expansion Writing `${CLAUDE_PLUGIN_ROOT:-.}` in a hook command substitutes to the **empty string**: So the harness treats `CLAUDE_PLUGIN_ROOT:-.` as a single unknown variable *name* and consumes the whole brace expression, rather than substituting the known variable and leaving the rest to the shell. Consequence: no standard shell parameter expansion (`:-`, `:+`, `%`, `#`) can be used anywhere in a hook command, because any brace expression containing an operator silently becomes empty. title: Show MCP server health and authentication status in the chat input
text: Show MCP server health and authentication status in the chat input. ## Feature request Show an indicator in or near the chat input when one or more enabled MCP servers need attention, including when a server: - is not signed in or otherwise requires authentication - is stuck starting - failed to initialize - encountered another error that prevents its tools from being available The indicator should make the affected server and its current state discoverable and provide a direct action to resolve the problem, such as signing in, retrying startup, viewing the error, or opening MCP configuration. It should avoid adding noise when all enabled servers are healthy. ## Motivation Today these failures can silently reduce the tools available to a chat session. A status affordance at the point of interaction would help users understand why an expected MCP tool is missing and recover without leaving the chat flow or hunting through logs/settings.

title: Enhance error handling and robustness in ApiProviderNaming ESLint rule during package.json loading

title: Make agent bake-offs available as an agent-invokable tool
text: Make agent bake-offs available as an agent-invokable tool. ## Motivation Agents should be able to run a bounded bake-off when a task would benefit from comparing multiple models, providers, agents, or configurations. Today this requires manual orchestration and the results are difficult to compare consistently. ## Proposal Expose an Agent Host tool that an agent can invoke to run the same task or evaluation prompt against a selected set of candidates and receive a structured comparison. The tool should support: - Selecting candidate models/providers/agents and an explicit task or evaluation prompt. - Running candidates in isolated child sessions so they cannot interfere with the current session or each other. - Configurable concurrency, timeout, and resource limits. - Consistent result capture, including outcome, summary, changed files/diff, validation results, duration, and available usage/cost signals. - A structured response that lets the calling agent compare results, explain trade

title: Make agent bake-offs available as an agent-invokable tool
text: ff, validation results, duration, and available usage/cost signals. - A structured response that lets the calling agent compare results, explain tradeoffs, and optionally recommend or adopt a winner. - Cancellation and reliable cleanup of child sessions/worktrees. - Clear handling for unavailable providers, partial failures, and candidates that require different capabilities. ## Questions to explore - What should the stable tool schema and result format be? - Which candidate dimensions should be supported initially: model, provider, custom agent, permission profile, or prompt variation? - How should success criteria be supplied and evaluated without allowing the judge to silently change the task? - Which telemetry and user-visible progress are needed? - What confirmation or policy gates are required before spawning multiple sessions or consuming significant resources? ## Done when - An agent can invoke the tool with a bounded candidate set. - Candidate runs are isolated, cancellable, a

title: Explore cross-platform pre-warming for agent worktrees
text: Explore cross-platform pre-warming for agent worktrees. ## Motivation Fresh worktree-isolated agent sessions currently defer worktree creation until the first send so the prompt can influence branch naming. That prevents the agent runtime and workspace-dependent caches from pre-warming, adding avoidable latency to the first turn. We should investigate whether worktrees can be provisioned or prepared earlier without sacrificing naming quality, correctness, or cleanup guarantees across Windows, macOS, and Linux. ## Investigation Explore a cross-platform design for pre-warming agent worktrees, including: - When pre-warming can start and which inputs are available before the first prompt. - Whether to create a provisional worktree/branch and rename it later, reserve a path, or split filesystem preparation from Git worktree creation. - Coordination with Agent Host/runtime pre-warming so providers do not materialize against a pending or incorrect working directory. - Cancellation, abandoned

title: Explore cross-platform pre-warming for agent worktrees
text: ation with Agent Host/runtime pre-warming so providers do not materialize against a pending or incorrect working directory. - Cancellation, abandoned composers, restart recovery, stale provisional worktrees, and deterministic cleanup. - Repository locking and races when multiple sessions pre-warm concurrently. - Windows path-length, file-locking, antivirus, junction/symlink, and case-sensitivity behavior. - macOS/Linux filesystem and symlink behavior, permissions, and performance differences. - Interaction with trust, remote workspaces, multi-root workspaces, submodules, sparse checkout, LFS, and `git.worktreeIncludeFiles`. - Disk usage and limits for speculative worktrees. ## Measurements Capture baseline and prototype timings for: - Composer open to worktree ready. - First send to provider dispatch. - First meaningful progress. - Cancellation and cleanup latency. Measure representative repositories on Windows, macOS, and Linux, including cold and warm filesystem/cache states. ## Done

title: Explore cross-platform pre-warming for agent worktrees
text: lation and cleanup latency. Measure representative repositories on Windows, macOS, and Linux, including cold and warm filesystem/cache states. ## Done when - We have a documented recommendation with platform-specific findings and identified risks. - A prototype demonstrates the viable lifecycle or proves why pre-warming should remain deferred. - The proposal defines state transitions, recovery/cleanup behavior, resource limits, and the integration point with provider pre-warming. - Follow-up implementation work is split into scoped issues as needed.

title: Diff editor toolbar can split Previous/Next Change actions when space is limited
text: Diff editor toolbar can split Previous/Next Change actions when space is limited. In the diff editor toolbar, **Previous Change** and **Next Change** can be split when the editor title area runs out of horizontal space. ### Steps to reproduce 1. On Windows, open a Git repository with both staged and unstaged changes. 2. Open a file from **Staged Changes**. Both navigation buttons are visible: - Previous Change (↑) - Next Change (↓) 3. Open a file from **Changes**. An additional editor-title action can appear. 4. With limited horizontal space, **Next Change** moves into the `...` overflow menu while **Previous Change** remains visible. ### Expected behavior Previous Change and Next Change are paired navigation controls. They should either: - Both remain visible, or - Both move into the overflow menu together. ### Actual behavior Only one of the paired controls remains visible, while the other moves into the overflow menu. This makes it look as though one navigation command is missing. #

A background subagent is actually waiting for explicit shell approval. Live debugging with the global `dbgjs` CLI confirmed that the SDK still knows the child and has its unresolved permission, but Agent Host no longer has the child's chat-routing registration. Child events, including the permission request, accumulate in `_pendingSubagentSignals` instead of reaching the client. title: MCP: show effective enablement state and scope
text: MCP: show effective enablement state and scope. context: https://vscodeteam.slack.com/archives/D0B3QD3C5FV/p1790102517578719 ## Problem The MCP UI shows different disabled states without explaining what they mean. A server can be globally disabled but enabled for the current workspace, while still showing a greyed-out disabled control. It is difficult to tell which servers are actually enabled in the current context and where that state comes from. ## Repro 1. Disable an MCP server globally. 2. Enable it for a specific workspace. 3. Inspect its state in the MCP UI and within a session in that workspace. ## Expected - Show the effective state for the current context, with labels such as `Enabled (Workspace)` or `Enabled (Session)`. - Distinguish the global default from workspace/session overrides. - Make disabled styling consistent and explain when a control is unavailable rather than representing an off state.

title: MCP: make default-off, per-workspace enablement easy to manage
text: MCP: make default-off, per-workspace enablement easy to manage. context: https://vscodeteam.slack.com/archives/D0B3QD3C5FV/p1790102517578719 ## Problem I want MCP servers disabled globally and to opt individual workspaces into the servers they need. Today, this means manually disabling every server, then re-enabling individual servers per workspace or session. There is not a clear place to see and manage those workspace choices. ## Expected - Provide an easy way to keep all MCP servers disabled by default as a user preference. - Enable selected servers for a workspace without changing the global default. - Make workspace overrides easy to inspect and remove. - Clearly distinguish session-only enablement from persistent workspace enablement. This is a request for a configurable workflow, not a change to the default for everyone.

title: Sending the first message to a remote session caused a different session to open
text: Sending the first message to a remote session caused a different session to open. this only happened once, right after creating a standalone agents tunnel on the remote. sending a new message was successful, but the wrong session was opened ## Reproduction 1. Use the Agents window with a remote Agent Host connected through a tunnel. 2. Create a new chat. Its backing session remains deferred until the first send. 3. Enter and send the first message while the tunnel connection is unstable or reconnecting. 🐛 unrelated chat opens while the message is sent to a new chat ## Correlated timeline - `10:59:39` — A new chat was created with deferred backing. - `11:02:53.112` — The Agent Host tunnel connection dropped while the first message was being submitted. - `11:02:53.388` — VS Code loaded the intended new session and began sending the request. - `11:02:53.515` — The reconnecting client refreshed the session catalogue. - The catalogue response omitted the still-deferred new session and retur

title: Sending the first message to a remote session caused a different session to open
text: - `11:02:53.515` — The reconnecting client refreshed the session catalogue. - The catalogue response omitted the still-deferred new session and returned the archived `Ping check` session as its first item. - `11:02:53.925` — The UI changed the shown session from the intended new session to `Ping check`. - `11:02:54.051` — The intended new session was treated as removed from the client-side session collection. - `11:02:54.063` — Session management reported that the active session had been replaced by the archived session. - `11:02:56.797` — The intended new session finished materializing. - `11:02:57.004` — The message was delivered to that correct new session, despite the UI displaying the archived one. ## Technical details The failure appears to be a reconciliation race between: - a locally known `isNewSession` whose Agent Host backing is still deferred; - tunnel reconnect and `listSessions` refresh; - first-send materialization; and - active-session fallback when the refreshed catal

title: Sending the first message to a remote session caused a different session to open
text: is still deferred; - tunnel reconnect and `listSessions` refresh; - first-send materialization; and - active-session fallback when the refreshed catalogue temporarily omits the pending session. This does not appear to be a message-routing failure. The send remained associated with the intended new session. The incorrect behavior is the client-side active-session replacement after the reconnect refresh. The relevant UI diagnostics explicitly show: - the archived session classified with reason `archived`; - the intended new session removed during the catalogue update; - the terminal transferred from the new session to the archived session; and - `sendRequest: active session replaced` from the new session to the archived one. ## Suggested safeguards - Preserve locally known pending/new sessions when a reconnect-time catalogue response temporarily omits them. - Pin the active session while its first request is materializing. - Do not fall back to an archived session when an active pending

text: arily omits them. - Pin the active session while its first request is materializing. - Do not fall back to an archived session when an active pending session disappears during reconciliation. - Add a regression test that disconnects the transport between first-message submission and `createSession` completion. ## Environment - VS Code Insiders - Remote Agent Host over a tunnel - Agents window / Copilot SDK provider - VS Code build commit visible in diagnostics: `a3b0c130bd` A diagnostic archive is available privately if needed, but it is intentionally not attached here because it contains full session logs.

title: Update agent prompts and skills for creating MCP configurations
text: Update agent prompts and skills for creating MCP configurations. ## Problem Agents need current, target-specific guidance when creating MCP configurations. In a recent Notion MCP setup, an agent wrote a VS Code-style configuration to `~/.copilot/mcp-config.json` using the top-level `servers` key, while the Copilot CLI/agent process expected `mcpServers`. The invalid configuration caused every new chat/session creation to fail with: Reinstalling VS Code did not resolve the failure because the broken configuration lived outside the VS Code installation and user-data paths. ## Proposed work Bring the prompts and skills used for MCP setup in line with the latest customization locations and formats: - Distinguish VS Code MCP configuration from Copilot CLI/agent-host configuration. - Select the correct destination and schema for the target client, including the correct top-level key (`servers` versus `mcpServers`). - Validate generated MCP configuration before reporting setup as complete. -

title: Update agent prompts and skills for creating MCP configurations
text: nt, including the correct top-level key (`servers` versus `mcpServers`). - Validate generated MCP configuration before reporting setup as complete. - Explain where the file was written and whether the relevant VS Code/Copilot process must be restarted. - Avoid adding unrelated troubleshooting settings when configuration validation fails. ## Acceptance criteria - Agent guidance identifies the target MCP consumer before editing configuration. - Generated configuration uses the schema required by that consumer. - The resulting file is parsed or otherwise validated before completion. - Guidance calls out configuration stored outside VS Code user-data paths so recovery steps are accurate.

title: Support env configuration in .mcp.json and migrate from .vscode/mcp.json
text: Support env configuration in .mcp.json and migrate from .vscode/mcp.json. ## Problem The new portable MCP configuration format uses repository-level `.mcp.json` files and user-level configuration under `.copilot`. These formats need a portable way to reference secrets and other machine-specific values. Existing VS Code workspaces commonly keep MCP configuration in `.vscode/mcp.json` and use `${input:...}` variables. Users need a clear migration path from that VS Code-specific format to the new `.mcp.json` format rather than extending `.vscode/mcp.json` further. Environment variables are the common mechanism supported by Copilot and Claude Code. Copilot's `${secret:...}` syntax is useful, but it is not part of a shared standard and therefore does not solve portability. Related ecosystem request: https://github.com/openai/codex/issues/38438 ## Proposal Provide first-class environment-variable references for MCP servers in: - Repository-level `.mcp.json` files. - User-level MCP configurat

title: Support env configuration in .mcp.json and migrate from .vscode/mcp.json
text: ## Proposal Provide first-class environment-variable references for MCP servers in: - Repository-level `.mcp.json` files. - User-level MCP configuration under `.copilot`. text: ibility/deprecation behavior so existing configurations do not break unexpectedly while users migrate. ## Expected outcome Users can check portable `.mcp.json` configurations into repositories, keep user-scoped MCP configuration under `.copilot`, and migrate away from `.vscode/mcp.json` without manually rewriting every server configuration or exposing secrets.

title: /btw took approximately 15.1 seconds from pressing Enter until the side chat began appearing in the UI
text: /btw took approximately 15.1 seconds from pressing Enter until the side chat began appearing in the UI. 1. long existing session 2. send a /btw message :bug: message is sent off, but takes a long time for anything to happen from copilot: **Bottom line:** `/btw` currently appears to synchronously cold-resume the source session, fork its history, and cold-resume the fork before the UI can display it. The best optimization target is the **fork path**, especially avoiding full-history inheritance/reconstruction when the source turn lookup fails and deferring changeset/MCP initialization until after the side chat is visible. the delay is clearly visible in the logs. It took approximately **15.1 seconds** from pressing Enter until the side chat began appearing in the UI. | Phase | Duration | What happened | |---|---:|---| | UI → host request | **~3 ms** | VS Code immediately issued `createChat`; the tunnel was not initially delaying the request. | | Resume source session | **~2.65 s** | The

title: /btw took approximately 15.1 seconds from pressing Enter until the side chat began appearing in the UI
text: **~3 ms** | VS Code immediately issued `createChat`; the tunnel was not initially delaying the request. | | Resume source session | **~2.65 s** | The host cold-resumed the original SDK session and reconstructed 17 turns from 2,906 persisted events. | | Fork source session | **~10.46 s** | Most of the delay occurred while creating the fork for `/btw`. | | Resume forked SDK session | **~1.44 s** | The new side-chat SDK session was initialized. | | Reconstruct/register chat | **~0.52 s** | The host loaded 2,912 events, announced the new chat, and completed `createChat`. | | UI load/render | **~29 ms** | VS Code subscribed to the new chat and created its UI model. | ### Main finding The bottleneck was **host-side side-chat creation**, particularly the **10.46-second fork phase**. It was not input handling, renderer work, network transit, or model inference. There is also a relevant warning: the requested source turn could not be found in the resumed session, so the fork **inherited all 17

title: /btw took approximately 15.1 seconds from pressing Enter until the side chat began appearing in the UI
text: odel inference. There is also a relevant warning: the requested source turn could not be found in the resumed session, so the fork **inherited all 17 turns** rather than forking cleanly at that turn. During the long fork interval, the host was also: - processing a large burst of customization/skill file-watcher events; - recomputing Git changesets for many historical turns; - running repeated Git commands; - initializing MCP servers, including an authentication-required server. The logs do not expose enough internal fork milestones to prove which of those consumed exactly how much of the 10.46 seconds. They do show that this work overlapped the fork and likely increased contention.

title: How Auto is displayed in experimental model picker
text: How Auto is displayed in experimental model picker. Some feedback on the new model picker design is that the section for Auto is too busy and is easily ignored. A couple of changes may help keep Auto a prominent option: - When Auto is enabled, collapse the rest of the model picker. No other models would show above it. This reduces the cognitive noise and keeps focus on Auto - When Auto is disabled, collapse the configuration options so it shows as one line item. We can keep the 10% discount showing but don't show the tiers until Auto is enabled. This uses progressive disclosure to keep the picker organized. I think these changes will also help with the introduction of HydraFusion. Where Auto shows as one line item, and HydraFusion shows directly below it. cc/ @bhavyaus

title: Chat session rename silently lost — never persisted, reverts within seconds, no reload/sleep needed
text: Chat session rename silently lost — never persisted, reverts within seconds, no reload/sleep needed. **Environment:** - VS Code: 1.138.0 (commit 7debcd0e2acdea1c52de81bf9ee1620444407dda) - Copilot Chat extension: 0.59.0 - Connection type: Remote - WSL - OS: Windows client + WSL (Linux) remote **Repro:** 1. Open an existing chat session with prior history (not a brand-new empty chat). 2. Rename it via the sidebar rename action (e.g. "Jira access and branch creation" → "Hydrn-3459 ..."). 3. Title updates immediately in the UI. 4. Within seconds — no reload, no sleep, single window — the title silently reverts to the pre-rename value. **Root cause evidence:** The chat session transcript is stored as an append-only .jsonl log at `%APPDATA%\Code\User\workspaceStorage\ \chatSessions\ .jsonl`, where a rename is recorded as an op: After reproducing the bug, I inspected the .jsonl for the affected session directly. The rename op for the new title does not exist anywhere in the file — only the o

title: Chat session rename silently lost — never persisted, reverts within seconds, no reload/sleep needed
text: ng the bug, I inspected the .jsonl for the affected session directly. The rename op for the new title does not exist anywhere in the file — only the original customTitle op is present. Since this file is append-only, if the rename had committed at all, the op would remain even if a later index rebuild reverted the displayed title. Its total absence means the write is lost before ever reaching persistent storage — this points to a race between the rename write and some other in-memory re-sync/refresh of the session title (rather than a debounce/flush timing issue), since it reproduces with a single window, no idle period, and no reconnect. **Impact:** Renamed session titles are unreliable — data loss of user-entered metadata, not just a display glitch.

title: Automations: support script-first actions with optional AI continuation
text: Automations: support script-first actions with optional AI continuation. ## Feature request Allow an automation to start by executing a script, before creating an AI session. The script should be able to complete the automation entirely without AI participation, or request that a new AI session be started. Conceptually, an automation could support an action such as `prompt | script`. A script action would perform deterministic work or checks first and decide whether AI is needed. ## Motivation Many automations can do useful work with a script alone, or cheaply determine that there is nothing for an agent to do. Starting an AI session for every trigger adds unnecessary cost and noise. Conversely, a script may discover work or encounter a failure for which AI assistance is useful. ## Independent outcomes Script success/failure and the decision to continue with AI should be independent, supporting all four combinations: | Script result | Start a new AI session? | Intended behavior | | ---

title: Automations: support script-first actions with optional AI continuation
text: ion to continue with AI should be independent, supporting all four combinations: | Script result | Start a new AI session? | Intended behavior | | --- | --- | --- | | Success | No | Complete the automation successfully without involving AI. | | Success | Yes | Start a new AI session with the script's output/context for follow-up work. | | Failure | No | Report the failed script/run without involving AI. | | Failure | Yes | Start a new AI session with the failure details for investigation or recovery; retain the script failure in the run history. | ## Expected behavior - Run the script before creating an AI session, not as a tool invocation inside an already-started AI session. - Provide an explicit, documented way to request or suppress AI continuation independently of the script's success/failure status. - When continuation is requested, allow a configured prompt and script output/context to be passed to the new session. - Preserve script output, errors, and exit status in the automat

title: Automations: support script-first actions with optional AI continuation
text: allow a configured prompt and script output/context to be passed to the new session. - Preserve script output, errors, and exit status in the automation run history, including runs that never create an AI session. - Surface invalid or missing control output and script execution errors explicitly, with documented behavior. ## Design question: signaling contract The exact protocol needs design. A special exit code (for example, `-2`) or a stdout marker such as `no-ai` could express "no AI needed", but a single special status conflates independent concerns, and free-form stdout markers may collide with ordinary output. Consider a structured result or dedicated control channel that expresses the AI-continuation decision separately from the process exit status. The request is for the four combinations above, not a particular exit code or marker. The design should also define how an AI follow-up affects the overall run status after a failed script.

title: Automations: optionally skip a run while a previous session is still running
text: Automations: optionally skip a run while a previous session is still running. ## Feature request Add an opt-in **skip if still running** option for automations. When a trigger fires and a session started by an earlier run of the same automation is still running, skip the new run instead of starting another session. ## Motivation Scheduled or frequently triggered automations can overlap when a previous session takes longer than the trigger interval. Users should be able to prevent duplicate work and competing changes without having to monitor sessions manually. ## Expected behavior - Make this configurable per automation; preserve the existing behavior when the option is disabled. - When enabled, check whether a session from an earlier run of that automation is still running before starting another session. - If so, skip this occurrence rather than queueing it or cancelling the existing session. - Show the occurrence as skipped, with the reason that an earlier session is still running.

title: Automations: optionally skip a run while a previous session is still running
text: ther than queueing it or cancelling the existing session. - Show the occurrence as skipped, with the reason that an earlier session is still running. - Once the previous session has finished, subsequent triggers can start sessions normally. - Apply the overlap guard atomically so simultaneous triggers cannot both start a session. The precise definition of "still running" (including sessions waiting for user input or approval) should be documented as part of the design.

title: Title: Copilot Chat agent emits unquoted Windows paths in terminal commands, triggering repeated OpenWith.exe dialogs on profile paths with spaces
text: Title: Copilot Chat agent emits unquoted Windows paths in terminal commands, triggering repeated OpenWith.exe dialogs on profile paths with spaces. Does this issue occur when all extensions are disabled?: No — this requires GitHub Copilot Chat (agent mode) to be enabled, since the bug is in the terminal commands the Copilot agent generates, not in VS Code core. Report Issue' dialog can assist with this. --> - VS Code Version: 1.138.0 (commit 7debcd0e2acdea1c52de81bf9ee1620444407dda, x64) - OS Version: Windows 10.0.26100.0 (Windows 11) Steps to Reproduce: 1. Use a Windows account whose profile path contains a space (e.g. display name "Max Mustermann" → `C:\Users\Max Mustermann`). 2. In Copilot Chat agent mode, give a task that leads the agent to open/reveal a file or folder under that profile path (e.g. anything likely to make it run `start `, `cmd /c start `, or `Invoke-Item ` without quoting it). 3. Observe the agent emits the path unquoted in the generated terminal command, e.g. `sta

title: Title: Copilot Chat agent emits unquoted Windows paths in terminal commands, triggering repeated OpenWith.exe dialogs on profile paths with spaces
text: t `, `cmd /c start `, or `Invoke-Item ` without quoting it). 3. Observe the agent emits the path unquoted in the generated terminal command, e.g. `start C:\Users\Max Mustermann\AppData\...`. 4. Because `start`/`Invoke-Item` `ShellExecute` their argument, the unquoted space splits the path at the first token (`C:\Users\Max Mustermann\...` → `C:\Users\Max `). Windows then tries to open a file literally named `Max` with no registered handler, and pops the `OpenWith.exe` "How do you want to open this file?" dialog. 5. Reproduced with `start` in both `cmd.exe` and PowerShell directly (outside the agent) — confirms this is standard Windows argument-splitting behavior once a path is unquoted, not a shell-specific quirk. **Impact:** each unquoted invocation produces its own dialog. When the agent runs several terminal commands in parallel or in quick succession that reference the same profile path, this can produce 10+ stacked `OpenWith.exe` dialogs in a single turn, all requiring manual dismi

title: Title: Copilot Chat agent emits unquoted Windows paths in terminal commands, triggering repeated OpenWith.exe dialogs on profile paths with spaces
text: uick succession that reference the same profile path, this can produce 10+ stacked `OpenWith.exe` dialogs in a single turn, all requiring manual dismissal, effectively blocking the session. **Expected behavior:** any terminal command the agent generates that embeds a filesystem path should always double-quote it, regardless of whether the path is already known to contain a space — this is a general shell-safety requirement (paths built from `%USERPROFILE%`/`$HOME`/user display names are not guaranteed to be space-free), not specific to this one repro case.

title: Perf: Agent Host per-request diff observable re-parses every historical turn on every streamed token in a long chat
text: Perf: Agent Host per-request diff observable re-parses every historical turn on every streamed token in a long chat. ## Summary While investigating a sustained VS Code Insiders renderer CPU spike in a long Agent Host chat session, the **Agent Host response-file-changes provider** was identified as the root trigger: it re-subscribes every historical request's file-change-diff observable to the whole chat's live streaming state, so **every streamed token of the active turn re-parses every prior turn's response into diffs again**. This is a distinct, upstream root cause from #337244 (which covers the downstream Prompt Timeline re-render symptom) — this issue is scoped to the Agent Host recompute that feeds it. ## Environment - macOS - VS Code Insiders 1.139.0-insider - distro/build: `8c7e9eebe250686ee086ffb96a4c570302ece3e3` - DevTools performance trace capturing a long chat session with an active streaming turn (repro is stable; the pattern repeats continuously for the session's duration

title: Perf: Agent Host per-request diff observable re-parses every historical turn on every streamed token in a long chat
text: rmance trace capturing a long chat session with an active streaming turn (repro is stable; the pattern repeats continuously for the session's duration, not just once at open) ## Perf evidence Renderer main-thread (`CrRendererMain`) aggregates from the trace: - `RunTask` 56,802.6 ms total, max 339.9 ms - **328 `RunTask` events ≥50 ms, totaling 44.53 s, over the final ~62.3 s of the trace (~71% of that window blocked)** - **303/328 of those long tasks contain `PromptTimelineGutterRail.setTicks` on the stack, totaling 42.04 s** - Long-task recurrence: median gap between starts **153.7 ms**, p90 **219.8 ms**, max 3644.3 ms — consistent with continuous token streaming, not a one-off event - A second renderer process (markdown webview) in the same trace had 31 ms total `RunTask` and zero tasks ≥50 ms — confirmed not causal - Inclusive CPU time on the diff/observable path: `_responsePartsToEntryDiffs` 5.12 s, `_diffsForRequest`/`getChangesForRequest` 4.36 s, `_statForRequests` 4.75 s - Self t

title: Perf: Agent Host per-request diff observable re-parses every historical turn on every streamed token in a long chat
text: on the diff/observable path: `_responsePartsToEntryDiffs` 5.12 s, `_diffsForRequest`/`getChangesForRequest` 4.36 s, `_statForRequests` 4.75 s - Self time: `set textContent` 4.4 s, `remove` 3.4 s, `_updateTabStops` 2.1 s, plus ~6–9 s across URI `parse`/`toString`/comparison helpers (`toAgentHostUri`/`toAgentHostContentUri`/`isEqual`/`getComparisonKey`) ## Root cause `_createDiffsObservable` unconditionally reads `responseFileEditsObs.read(reader)` near the top of every recompute — even when a stable `changeset` or `branchFallback` source already wins for that request. That unconditional read wires **every** historical request's diff observable to `_createFileEditDiffsObservable`, which: 1. subscribes to the chat's `ChatStateSubscription`, whose `onDidChange` fires on every reducer action that mutates `state.activeTurn` — i.e. every streamed token/tool-call/reasoning delta of the turn currently in progress, and 2. does an **O(N) `chatState.turns.find(turn => turn.id === requestId)`** loo

title: Perf: Agent Host per-request diff observable re-parses every historical turn on every streamed token in a long chat
text: d token/tool-call/reasoning delta of the turn currently in progress, and 2. does an **O(N) `chatState.turns.find(turn => turn.id === requestId)`** lookup, then fully re-parses that turn's `responseParts` into a **brand-new object every time**, with no memoization. Since `derived()`'s default equality is `strictEquals`, this new-object-every-time result always reports "changed" downstream, regardless of whether the request's actual diffs are unchanged. **Why this is fixable cheaply:** the chat reducer's `endTurn` (reducer.ts) only ever appends to `state.turns` — no action mutates an existing entry. Completed turn objects are therefore **reference-stable** for the rest of the session, so an identity-keyed cache (keyed on the resolved `turn` object) is sufficient; no deep equality is required. ## Regression history (git blame) Two distinct commits contributed, both from the same author: - **Original O(N) lookup** (baked in from initial design, not itself a regression): `3cedee308d2` / #32

title: Perf: Agent Host per-request diff observable re-parses every historical turn on every streamed token in a long chat
text: ommits contributed, both from the same author: - **Original O(N) lookup** (baked in from initial design, not itself a regression): `3cedee308d2` / #325037 *"chat: show turn previews as resource labels"* — introduced `_createFileEditDiffsObservable` and its `turns.find` lookup as a narrow fallback path. - **Proximate regression — the unconditional top-of-function read**: `d52881e2e42e`, line 215 / **#334465** *"agentHost: Keep Agent Merge notice changesets empty"*, merged **2026-09-04** (~18 days before this trace). Diffing that commit shows it moved `const responseFileEdits = responseFileEditsObs.read(reader);` from **after** the `changeset`/`branchFallback`/`authoritativeEmpty` early-return checks to **unconditionally at the top**, in order to add a new `isHostNotice` early exit. Before this commit, a request already settled by an authoritative changeset never touched the expensive response-parsing path at all; after it, every request subscribes to and re-evaluates the live active-tur

title: Perf: Agent Host per-request diff observable re-parses every historical turn on every streamed token in a long chat
text: itative changeset never touched the expensive response-parsing path at all; after it, every request subscribes to and re-evaluates the live active-turn stream on every token. ## Suggested fix - Memoize `_createFileEditDiffsObservable`'s result keyed on the resolved `turn` object reference (turns are reference-stable once appended to `state.turns`), so unrelated historical requests short-circuit to a cached, reference-equal result instead of re-parsing on every token. - Replace the per-request O(N) `turns.find` with one shared `Map ` built once per `ChatState` change and reused across all N per-request observables (turns O(N·M) work per streamed token into O(M) shared + O(1) per request). ## Relationship to #337244 #337244 already covers the downstream symptom in the Prompt Timeline (`ticks`/`promptTicks` derived observables with no equality function, and `PromptTimelineGutterRail.setTicks` unconditionally re-rendering every row). That issue's own evidence is a one-time double-render du

title: Perf: Agent Host per-request diff observable re-parses every historical turn on every streamed token in a long chat
text: ty function, and `PromptTimelineGutterRail.setTicks` unconditionally re-rendering every row). That issue's own evidence is a one-time double-render during session open/history-restore (~524 ms total across 2 tasks), separate from this issue's mechanism (continuous re-trigger during live token streaming, 44.53 s across 328 tasks in this trace). Fixing #337244 alone would mask the redundant DOM re-render, but this provider would still re-parse every historical turn's `responseParts` on every streamed token — the CPU cost upstream of the render would remain. Both fixes together are needed to eliminate the sustained spike end-to-end. ## Suggested regression test In `agentHostResponseFileChanges.test.ts`: observe a historical (already-completed) turn's diffs via the existing `autorun` test harness, then fire N active-turn-only `ChatState` updates (e.g. streamed tool-call deltas on a *different*, later turn) and assert the historical turn's observed diffs array keeps **reference equality** a

title: Three-finger swipe down no longer shows recent files after updating to macOS 27
text: Three-finger swipe down no longer shows recent files after updating to macOS 27. Does this issue occur when all extensions are disabled?: Yes * VS Code Version: 1.138.0 (Universal) * OS Version: macOS 27 ### Steps to Reproduce 1. Use the macOS three-finger swipe-down gesture while the VS Code window is active. 2. Before updating to macOS 27, this gesture displayed the recently opened files for VS Code, allowing quick switching between them. 3. After updating to macOS 27, the gesture no longer shows the recent files. ### Expected Behavior The three-finger swipe-down gesture should display the recent files/windows associated with VS Code, as it did on previous macOS versions. ### Actual Behavior After updating to macOS 27, performing the gesture in VS Code no longer displays the recent files.

text: Perf: pending-confirmation detection does two full O(N) response scans per notification (restore and live streaming). ## Summary While investigating a renderer CPU spike reported when opening a very long Copilot session ("Session database redesing"), the root cause traced to the pending-confirmation/approval detection path: on every non-quiet response change, two independent full linear scans of the response's part array run — one inside `ChatResponseModel.isPendingConfirmation` (`chatModel.ts`), and a second, redundant one inside `AgentSessionApprovalModel._trackModel`'s autorun (`agentSessionApprovalModel.ts`). The specific O(N²) blowup that made this visible — replaying every historical response part as its own non-quiet notification during session restore — has already been fixed separately (batched restore now fires one notification instead of N). This issue is about what's left: **the scan itself is still O(N) per notification**, which matters for: - The single "final" notificati

text: instead of N). This issue is about what's left: **the scan itself is still O(N) per notification**, which matters for: - The single "final" notification after a long restore (still one full pass over every part). - Live streaming of a long response, where most `updateContent` calls are intentionally non-quiet (the user needs to see them), so a response with many streamed parts pays an O(N) rescan on every token/part added — effectively O(N²) over the life of one long-running turn, independent of restore. ## Perf evidence From the original trace: the dominant 2.19s long task's stack bottomed out in `readObservable` (~4463 samples / 581.7 ms self time) under an anonymous observable computation that maps to `agentSessionApprovalModel.ts` (`_trackModel`'s `autorun`). `UpdateLayoutTree` (435.5 ms total, max 4.3 ms) and `Paint` (86.5 ms total, max 1.6 ms) were negligible by comparison — this is synchronous JS/observable work, not rendering. ## Analysis `ChatResponseModel.isPendingConfirmatio

title: Perf: pending-confirmation detection does two full O(N) response scans per notification (restore and live streaming)
text: max 1.6 ms) were negligible by comparison — this is synchronous JS/observable work, not rendering. ## Analysis `ChatResponseModel.isPendingConfirmation` (see chatModel.ts, the `_pendingInfo` derived value in the constructor): `signal` is an `observableSignalFromEvent` over `this.onDidChange`, which fires on every non-quiet `updateContent`/`_contentChanged` call. So this full-array scan re-runs on every streamed token/part for as long as the response is open, not just at restore. `AgentSessionApprovalModel._trackModel` (see agentSessionApprovalModel.ts) then does its own **second** full scan immediately after reading `isPendingConfirmation`: This second loop re-finds the same toolInvocation part that `_pendingInfo` already located internally (to build the UI-specific label/kind/terminal detection), duplicating the first scan's work rather than reusing its result. It's also nested inside the outer `for (const request of requests.read(reader).toReversed())` loop, which walks every retaine

title: Perf: pending-confirmation detection does two full O(N) response scans per notification (restore and live streaming)
text: than reusing its result. It's also nested inside the outer `for (const request of requests.read(reader).toReversed())` loop, which walks every retained request looking for the first one needing input. ## Suggested direction (for consideration, not prescriptive) - Consider having `isPendingConfirmation` (or a sibling observable) expose the located part reference itself, so `AgentSessionApprovalModel` can reuse it directly instead of re-scanning `response.response.value` a second time. - Consider whether `_pendingInfo`'s scan can avoid re-walking from index 0 on every signal fire — e.g. tracking the last-scanned length/part and only inspecting newly appended parts, since a response's part array only grows monotonically between `clear()`/`reopen()` calls. - Preserve existing semantics: both loops currently return on the *first* qualifying part found (array order matters), and the outer loop in `_trackModel` prefers the current request before older retained-agent responses — any incrementa

title: Perf: prompt timeline gutter/ruler re-renders every row and recomputes diff stats twice when opening a long session
text: Perf: prompt timeline gutter/ruler re-renders every row and recomputes diff stats twice when opening a long session. ## Summary While investigating a renderer CPU spike reported when opening a very long Copilot session ("Session database redesing"), the prompt timeline (gutter/ruler rail) was identified as a **secondary** contributor: it re-renders every timeline row and recomputes every request's diff stats **twice** while a long session is opened, even though nothing about most rows actually changed between the two passes. The primary cause (an O(N²) observable-notification cascade in the response/approval model during history restore) has already been fixed separately. This issue is scoped to the timeline-specific cost so it can be reviewed/fixed by the timeline's owner. ## Environment (from the original report) - macOS - VS Code Insiders 1.139.0-insider - distro/build: `8c7e9eebe250686ee086ffb96a4c570302ece3e3` - Two DevTools performance traces captured opening the long session, bo

text: so this is DOM/JS work in the row-rendering path, not layout or paint ## Analysis `PromptTimelineModel` derives `ticks` / `promptTicks` (see promptTimelineModel.ts) from the chat view model plus each request's diff stat (`_statForRequests` → `_diffsForRequest` → `IChatResponseFileChangesService.getChangesForRequest`). During history restore: 1. The underlying view model fires multiple change notifications while requests/responses are being populated (this is also being reduced by the separate approval-model fix, but the timeline observable recomputes on every one of them regardless). 2. Each recompute previously produced a **new array of tick objects** even when the tick contents were structurally identical to the previous pass, because the derived observables had no custom equality function — a plain reference/array identity check always says "changed". 3. `PromptTimelineGutterRail.setTicks` / `PromptTimelineRulerRail.setTicks` then re-render **every** row/mark unconditionally for a "

text: says "changed". 3. `PromptTimelineGutterRail.setTicks` / `PromptTimelineRulerRail.setTicks` then re-render **every** row/mark unconditionally for a "same structure" tick list (see the loops calling `_renderRow(this._rows[i], ticks[i])` / `_renderMark(this._marks[i], ticks[i])` for every index), which re-touches every row's DOM (`textContent`, `clearNode`, `setAttribute`) and recomputes every request's diff stat again via `_statForRequests`, even for rows whose stat/text/timestamp didn't change. Net effect: for a session with many prompts, opening it can pay for a full row+stat rebuild of the entire timeline more than once, which is O(N) work repeated multiple times for no visible change. ## Suggested direction (for consideration, not prescriptive) - Give the `ticks` / `promptTicks` derived observables a structural equality function so a recompute that produces the same tick values is a no-op for downstream consumers. - In `setTicks`, skip re-rendering (and re-computing the stat DOM fo

title: Scrollbars on Terminal, Debug Output, etc. panels need buttons for precision scrolling
text: Scrollbars on Terminal, Debug Output, etc. panels need buttons for precision scrolling. The lack of scroll buttons is a serious problem in output windows like the Terminal and Debug Output panels where precision scrolling is *required* to navigate long output. Because the cursor does not move the view of the content in these panels, it is not possible to arrow through it line-by-line the way you can in the editor. The lack of precision control makes it very difficult (borderline impossible in some cases) to bring specific parts of the output into view. I don't know if gestures or a mouse wheel scroll in smaller intervals, but those aren't viable options for me. I'm using a touchpad, and I disable gestures/tapping because I find they trigger accidentally so often that the problems they cause vastly outweigh any benefits. Not to mention that getting them to trigger when they're needed is unreliable. (My difficulties with gestures and tapping may or may not be related to my arthritis.) #

title: Agent host applies the CAPI proxy to all Copilot CLI requests,   breaking MCP to PAC-DIRECT hosts
text: Agent host applies the CAPI proxy to all Copilot CLI requests, breaking MCP to PAC-DIRECT hosts. - VS Code Version: **1.138.0** (commit `7debcd0e2acdea1c52de81bf9ee1620444407dda`) - OS Version: Linux x64 - Does this issue occur when all extensions are disabled?: **Yes** (the agent host and the bundled Copilot CLI are built in) ## Summary When the OS proxy is configured through a PAC script and no explicit proxy settings or proxy environment variables are present, the agent host resolves the proxy for a **single** URL — `api.githubcopilot.com`, or whatever `resolveApiEndpoint()` returns — and writes that one result into the Copilot CLI subprocess as `HTTP_PROXY`/`HTTPS_PROXY`. Every HTTP request that subprocess makes is then forced through a proxy chosen only for an external endpoint, **including MCP requests to hosts the PAC script explicitly maps to `DIRECT`**. ## Relationship to #326185 / #333614 — this is the remaining case, not a duplicate I can confirm **#333614 works as intended

text: itly maps to `DIRECT`**. ## Relationship to #326185 / #333614 — this is the remaining case, not a duplicate I can confirm **#333614 works as intended on 1.138.0**. On the same machine, same day: `http.noProxy` is now forwarded, and `_readNoProxy()` additionally falls back to an inherited `no_proxy`/`NO_PROXY`. That fixed our symptom once we set `http.noProxy` explicitly. What remains is the path #333614 deliberately left in place — *"OS/PAC discovery remains the final fallback"*. On that path there is **no bypass list to forward**, because PAC does not expose one (see below), so a single collapsed proxy value is still applied process-wide. A clean machine with only a PAC and no explicit settings therefore still fails on 1.138.0. ## Why PAC makes this incorrect by construction PAC has no bypass *list*. `FindProxyForURL(url, host)` answers **per host**, and the answer may depend on `dnsResolve()`, `myIpAddress()` or arbitrary JavaScript. Collapsing one host's answer into a process-wide v

Collapsing one host's answer into a process-wide value discards the function's entire purpose — and there is no list that could be forwarded as `NO_PROXY` instead. An anonymised PAC equivalent to the one in our environment: What it returns for the two hosts that matter: | Target | PAC answer | | --- | --- | | `api.githubcopilot.com` | `PROXY proxy-external.corp.example:3128` | | `internal-mcp.corp.example` | `DIRECT` — matches `*.corp.example`, and its address is in `10.0.0.0/8` | The subprocess receives `HTTP_PROXY=http://proxy-external.corp.example:3128` and sends the internal request there. That proxy has no route into the internal network, so the request times out. The PAC's `DIRECT` answer for the internal host is never queried on this code path. ## Steps to Reproduce All of the following must hold — on 1.138.0 any one of them is enough to mask the problem: 1. Rows 2 and 3 are the two independent ways out, which is what isolates the cause: the failure is not "a proxy is in the way", it is "a proxy chosen for a different host was applied to this one". ## Root cause (code as of 1.138.0) `src/vs/platform/agentHost/node/copilot/copilotAgent.ts`: The intent looks narrow — the log message says "to Copilot SDK" — but the mechanism is a process-wide environment variable, so the effective scope is every HTTP client in that subprocess.
